\section[la celebración]{la celebración — the celebration}

\label{lesson:ES-C558-celebracion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the coffin, then the Spanish for the inheritance.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la celebración}
\textbf{la celebración} — \textquotedblleft{}the celebration\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La celebración duró hasta las tres.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The celebration went on until three.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{celebración} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{celebrātiō} 'a crowded gathering, a festival' (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{celebrāre} 'to fill, to celebrate'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la celebración}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la celebración}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la celebración}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the coffin, then the Spanish for the inheritance, then say \emph{la celebración} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la celebración mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The celebration\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[festejar]{festejar — to celebrate, to party}

\label{lesson:ES-C558-festejar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the inheritance, then the Spanish for the celebration.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: festejar}
\textbf{festejar} — \textquotedblleft{}to celebrate, to party\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Festejamos el cumpleaños de la abuela en el jardín.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We celebrated grandma's birthday in the garden.}
\end{quote}

Very common in Latin America; \emph{celebrar} is used everywhere.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{festejar} is built on \emph{fiesta}, from Latin \emph{fēsta}, the plural of \emph{fēstum} 'a feast day' (Lewis \& Short), with the ending \emph{-ejar}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{festejar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{festejar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{festejar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the inheritance, then the Spanish for the celebration, then say \emph{festejar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does festejar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To celebrate, to party\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[conmemorar]{conmemorar — to commemorate}

\label{lesson:ES-C558-conmemorar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the celebration, then the Spanish for to celebrate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: conmemorar}
\textbf{conmemorar} — \textquotedblleft{}to commemorate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El pueblo conmemora aquel día cada año.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The town commemorates that day every year.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{conmemorar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{commemorāre} 'to call to mind' (EtymDB), built on \emph{con-} and \emph{memorāre} 'to recall', from \emph{memor} 'mindful'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el homenaje]{el homenaje — the tribute, the homage}

\label{lesson:ES-C558-homenaje}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to celebrate, then the Spanish for to commemorate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el homenaje}
\textbf{el homenaje} — \textquotedblleft{}the tribute, the homage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Le hicieron un homenaje al viejo profesor.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They held a tribute to the old teacher.}
\end{quote}

\emph{En homenaje a} — in honour of.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{homenaje} is usually traced to Occitan or Catalan \emph{homenatge}, built on the word for 'man', from Latin \emph{homō} (Lewis \& Short). Homage was the vow of a lord's man.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el homenaje}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el homenaje}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to celebrate, then the Spanish for to commemorate, then say \emph{el homenaje} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el homenaje mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The tribute, the homage\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[inaugurar]{inaugurar — to open, to inaugurate}

\label{lesson:ES-C558-inaugurar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to commemorate, then the Spanish for the tribute.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: inaugurar}
\textbf{inaugurar} — \textquotedblleft{}to open, to inaugurate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El alcalde inauguró la nueva biblioteca.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The mayor opened the new library.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{inaugurar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{inaugurāre} 'to take omens from the flight of birds' (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{augur}, the priest who read the birds before anything new began.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to commemorate, then the Spanish for the tribute, then say \emph{inaugurar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
